newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank Canada's Thiessen rejects call for higher inflation.
newsitem.headline: Bank Canada's Thiessen rejects call for higher inflation.

text.p: Bank of Canada Gov. Gordon Thiessen said on Wednesday he had no plans to alter the central bank's tough stand on inflation.
The central bank governor also forecast that the Canadian economy will strengthen in the coming year, benefiting from the country's lowest interest rates in 40 years.

"I am convinced that the Canadian economy is on the right path. The benefits of the economic transformation we have undertaken are on the way. We just need to stay the course," Thiessen told a business gathering.

In his speech, Thiessen rejected recent calls for the Bank of Canada to raise its inflation targets. Some economists have argued that if the central bank allowed a higher inflation rate, it would grease the wheels of the economy and lower Canada's 9.9 percent unemployment rate.

Canada's inflation rate of about 1.2 percent is among the lowest in the world and less than half the U.S. inflation rate. The Bank of Canada's target range for the inflation rate is 1.0 percent to 3.0 percent.

Thiessen said he did not believe a higher inflation rate would result in more growth and employment. The governor said that if the central bank softened its tough stand on inflation, the hard-won benefits of the policy would be quickly lost.

Among the benefits cited by Thiessen was the central bank's increased ability to control short-term interest rates. The Bank of Canada has cut Canadian rates 10 times this year in a bid to spur Canada's anaemic economy. Nine of the cuts were independent of the U.S. Federal Reserve.

Canada's key bank rate, which is similar to the U.S. discount rate, is at 3.5 percent, its lowest level since August 1963. The Bank of Canada has cut short-term interest rates by 4.75 percentage points since May 1995. The 5 percent prime rate charged by Canada's commercial banks is the lowest since July 1956.
Thiessen said the drop in interest rates, which was due partly to Canada's low inflation, would soon spur Canadian economic growth.

"I believe that it is only a matter of time before this monetary easing encourages a resurgence in household spending," said Thiessen. "While the improvements have been slow in coming and our unemployment rate remains high, the economic outlook is favourable."
